# Conclusions

While vectorization could have provided an ideal solution to find "key insights" in clinical notes of patients with ovarian cancer that directly relate to new understanding of early symptoms or risk factors of subsequent ovarian cancer diagnosis, our results show this approach is far too noisy to yield clear and meaningful results. These types of approaches may be best suited to draw out themes that could be explicitly tested for in subssequent research. Importantly, these approaches need tools to reduce manual review, such as custom lists of "Stop words" that apply to specific-contexts, allowing customization of words and phrases to ignore depending on the domain. 

Our second method, embedding of clinical notes and use in a Random Forest model, yielded poor results as well. Accuracy of these models ranged from 55-59%, which is barely better than random chance. It is possible this is due to the need for data to be analyzed differently, perhaps with a machine learning model that can better account for an individual's sequential health journey or the addition of structured features to be analyzed with unstructured features. It is also possible, there is not a clear prediction signal in the clinical notes to predict subsequent ovarian cancer diagnosis. 

Our analysis is limited by intentional scope, which did not explore deep learning models or the inclusion of structured features, such as medication or diagnosis information alongside unstructured data. Natural future steps would be to implement both, starting with the integration of the structured features. Future analyses would benefit from maintaining optimally parsimonious models, so insight in source of prediction could be understood and applied to clinical practice.
